chapters.title: Frames on the Block
chapters.blurb: It is opening morning in Packet Alley. The noodle shop, its printers, and the nearby desks share one local network. Before anyone can depend on it, you need to find out what each device knows.

chapters.title: Routes Across Town
chapters.blurb: The local network is running. Now the shop needs services on the other side of the city. Each router makes its own forwarding decision. Your job is to read those decisions before changing them.

chapters.title: Handshakes and Delivery
chapters.blurb: Messages can cross the city. The remaining problem is keeping a conversation open long enough to finish the work. The service desk needs a connection, and the shop needs complete files.

chapters.title: When Too Much Arrives
chapters.blurb: The night market is open. The city is busy, and a small server receives more requests than its link can carry. Your assignment is to observe what fails and explain the evidence.

levels.title: The kitchen order
levels.story: The noodle shop is open. The kitchen printer has gone quiet, and the orders are waiting at the counter.
concept: Every device on a block has its own IP address.
A packet carries the address of where it is going.
Send to the right address and the switch delivers it.
levels.task: Inspect the computer, printer, and switch. Prepare the order for delivery without changing the wrong machine.

edits.prompt: Where should the order go?

goal.text: The printer receives all three orders.

bonus.text: No frame is lost along the way.

quiz.question: Why did the first order each run reach the printer even though the switch had never seen it before?
options: The switch floods a frame out of every other port until it learns where a device is.
The printer shouted its address first.
Switches know every address in advance.
quiz.why: A switch that does not yet know a destination sends the frame everywhere, then remembers which port the replies come back on.

levels.debrief: The first order reached the kitchen. The shop can work again.

levels.title: Lunch rush
levels.story: Two registers send their totals at once. The old wiring loses both. Lunch is coming, and the owner wants an explanation before buying new equipment.
concept: A hub repeats every frame out of every other port.
Only one device can talk at a time; two at once collide.
A switch gives each device its own line, so they do not collide.
levels.task: Inspect the two incoming links and the middle device. Decide what change will let both tills report at the same time.

edits.prompt: What should the middle box be?

goal.text: No collisions happen.
Register A's four sales arrive.
Register B's four sales arrive.

quiz.question: Why does a switch let both registers send at the same time?
options: It sends each frame only out of the one port its destination is on, so the two never share a wire.
It is faster, so collisions do not matter.
It tells one register to wait.
quiz.why: Because a switch forwards each frame to just the right port, two conversations can cross it at once without meeting.

levels.debrief: The totals arrived. The owner has a working shop and a reason for the change.

levels.title: The backup line
levels.story: A spare cable was installed overnight. Since then, the printer receives repeated copies of the same message.
concept: Two switches joined by two cables make a loop.
A flooded frame goes around the loop forever, copying itself.
Blocking one of the two cables breaks the loop (this is what spanning tree does).
levels.task: Trace both paths between the switches. Choose a port to block while keeping the printer connected.

edits.prompt: The spare cable between the switches:

goal.text: The print job reaches the printer.
No more than 12 frames cross a cable (a storm makes far more).

quiz.question: What makes the single print job turn into a storm when both cables are active?
options: The switches flood the frame to each other over both cables, and each copy is flooded again, with no hop limit to stop it.
The printer keeps asking for it.
The front desk sent it many times.
quiz.why: A frame on a loop has nothing to kill it — unlike an IP packet, a frame has no hop count — so it multiplies until something blocks a path.

levels.debrief: The repeated traffic stopped. One route remains open to the printer.

levels.title: Four registers
levels.story: The noodle shop opened two more registers. Now the old boxes are losing sales during the busiest part of the day.
concept: A hub is one shared wire: only one device can talk at a time.
Two frames arriving together on a hub collide, and both are lost — and the more machines share a hub, the more often that happens.
A switch gives every machine its own line, so a whole crowd can talk at once without colliding.
levels.task: Inspect both middle boxes. Make a plan for the shared lines before replacing anything.

edits.prompt: The front box should be:
The back box should be:

goal.text: No sale collides with another.
Register A's sales all arrive.
Register C's sales all arrive.

quiz.question: You had four registers this time instead of two. What does adding more machines to a hub do?
options: It makes collisions more likely, because they all share one wire and only one can talk at a time.
Nothing — a hub gives each machine its own line.
It speeds the hub up to keep pace.
quiz.why: Every machine on a hub shares the one wire, so the more of them there are, the more often two talk at once and collide. A switch is what lets a crowd grow.

levels.debrief: Every register reported its sales. There is enough room to serve the queue.

levels.title: The duplicate paths
levels.story: The shop added backup cables between the service rooms. Traffic now circles through both ends of the building.
concept: Two switches joined by two cables make a loop, and a flooded frame rides a loop forever, copying itself.
Each spare cable here adds its own loop, so each one has to be dealt with.
Blocking one end of a spare cable breaks that loop while leaving the real path intact — this is what spanning tree does automatically.
levels.task: Find every closed forwarding path. Leave a working route between the desk and printer.

edits.prompt: The spare cable between Switch 1 and Switch 2:
The spare cable between Switch 2 and Switch 3:

goal.text: The print job reaches the printer.
No more than 16 frames cross a cable (a storm makes far more).

quiz.question: Why did leaving even one spare cable active still cause a storm?
options: Each pair of cables is its own loop, and one open loop is enough for a flooded frame to circle and multiply forever.
The printer asked for the job twice.
Two spare cables cancel each other out, but one does not.
quiz.why: A loop needs no partner to run away: one unbroken loop lets a frame copy itself without end. Every redundant link is its own loop to break.

levels.debrief: The backbone is stable. The backup cables are still there, ready for a failed primary link.

levels.title: Open the upstairs floor
levels.story: Upstairs opens in an hour. Three desks need the server, and the contractor left the network half configured.
concept: A real segment has to get every part right at once: no shared-wire hubs where machines collide, and no unbroken loop where frames storm.
Swap each hub for a switch so every machine has its own line.
Block the one spare cable so the backbone has no loop.
levels.task: Inspect the boxes, links, and test traffic. Sign off only when the network serves every desk.

edits.prompt: Box 1 should be:
Box 2 should be:
The spare cable on the backbone:

goal.text: No frames collide.
Desk 1 is served.
Desk 3 is served.
No more than 90 frames cross a cable (an unbroken loop makes far more).

quiz.question: A working segment needs both fixes. What is each one guarding against?
options: Switches stop machines colliding on a shared wire; blocking the spare stops frames storming around a loop.
Both fixes do the same thing, so either alone is enough.
Switches prevent loops and blocking cables prevents collisions.
quiz.why: They solve different faults: a hub causes collisions because its machines share one wire, and an open loop causes a storm because a frame can circle forever. A healthy segment has neither.

levels.debrief: The new floor is ready. You can hear the printers working above the shop.

levels.title: The other side of the street
levels.story: A customer at the shop needs a document stored across the street. The computer can see its local network, but nothing beyond it.
concept: A device talks to its own block directly.
For anywhere else, it hands the packet to its gateway — the router.
The gateway must be an address on the device's own block.
levels.task: Inspect the client address, subnet, and both sides of the router. Set a reachable first hop.

edits.prompt: The shop PC's gateway:

goal.text: All three pings get a reply.

quiz.question: Why must the gateway be 10.0.1.1 and not 10.0.2.1?
options: The PC can only hand a packet to an address on its own block (10.0.1.0/24); the router's near side is on that block.
Lower numbers are always closer.
The server chose it.
quiz.why: To reach anywhere else the PC first has to deliver the packet to the router, and it can only do that on the block they share.

levels.debrief: The reply came back across the street. The client can reach the other block.

levels.title: A missing direction
levels.story: The market server answers messages. The shop router simply does not know how to reach it.
concept: A router keeps a table: for each destination block, the next hop.
A block it is plugged into needs no route — it is directly connected.
For a block further away, it forwards to the next router.
levels.task: Trace the outward and return paths. Add the missing forwarding entry to the near router.

edits.prompt: Router 1's route to the server's block (10.0.2.0/24):

goal.text: All three pings get a reply.

quiz.question: Router 2 was never given a route to the server's block. How does it still deliver there?
options: It is plugged directly into that block, so it is a connected route — no table entry needed.
It floods the packet everywhere.
Router 1 told it where to go.
quiz.why: A router always knows the blocks it is directly attached to. Routes are only needed for blocks it cannot see directly.

levels.debrief: A route now leads to the market. Both directions of the exchange are visible on the map.

levels.title: A message going in circles
levels.story: The shop router and the middle router keep sending the same request back to each other. It never reaches the far server.
concept: Every IP packet starts with a hop count (TTL).
Each router it crosses subtracts one.
At zero the packet is dropped — this is what stops a routing loop from lasting forever.
levels.task: Read the forwarding entries. Break the cycle before the request runs out of hops.

edits.prompt: Router 1's route to the far block (10.0.2.0/24):

goal.text: All three pings get a reply.

bonus.text: No packet runs out of hops.

quiz.question: What would happen without a hop count if Router 1 and the middle router kept pointing at each other?
options: The packet would bounce between them forever, wasting the link.
It would eventually find its own way.
Nothing — routers never loop.
quiz.why: The hop count is the safety net: a misconfigured loop still ends, because every router subtracts one and the packet dies at zero.

levels.debrief: The request has a path out of town. The repeated trip through the middle is over.

levels.title: Two missing settings
levels.story: The riverside server is online. The shop cannot reach it, and two devices have incomplete instructions.
concept: A device reaches its own block directly; for anywhere else it hands the packet to its gateway, which must sit on its own block.
A router forwards by its table: for each far-off block, the next router toward it.
Set the hand-off and the signpost, and the packet finds its way.
levels.task: Examine the client and the near router separately. Repair the handoff and the onward route.

edits.prompt: The shop PC's gateway (its way off the block):

options.label: The near router, here on our block (10.0.1.1)
The far router, over the bridge (10.0.3.1)

edits.prompt: The near router's signpost for the server's block (10.0.3.0/24):

goal.text: All three pings get a reply.

quiz.question: The far router was never given a signpost for the server's block, yet it still delivered there. Why?
options: It is plugged straight into that block, so it is directly connected — no table entry needed.
The near router told it the way.
It floods the packet out of every port.
quiz.why: A router always knows the blocks it is wired to. Signposts (routes) are only for blocks it cannot see directly — like the near router needed for the server's block.

levels.debrief: The riverside answered. Both missing settings are now accounted for.

levels.title: Market or harbor
levels.story: The shop sends receipts to the market and orders to the harbor. One junction serves both, but its signs are missing.
concept: A routing table is a list of signposts: for each destination block, which road leads there.
Point a block down the wrong road and the packet reaches a router that cannot deliver it — and it is dropped.
Each block needs its own correct signpost.
levels.task: Inspect each destination network. Give the junction a separate forwarding decision for each one.

edits.prompt: The junction's signpost for the market block (10.0.2.0/24):
The junction's signpost for the harbour block (10.0.3.0/24):

goal.text: Both market pings get a reply.
Both harbour pings get a reply.

bonus.text: No packet is sent down a dead end.

quiz.question: What happens if the junction sends the harbour block down the market road?
options: The market router receives it, has no way to the harbour block, and drops it.
The market router passes it along until it finds the harbour.
It arrives anyway — any road reaches any block.
quiz.why: A router only knows the blocks it is wired to and the signposts it was given. Sent the wrong way, a packet reaches a router that cannot deliver it, and there the journey ends.

levels.debrief: Both neighborhoods answered. No message took the wrong road.

levels.title: The far-side delivery
levels.story: The final shipment report must cross the entire city before the market opens. Three routers stand between the shop and the archive.
concept: A packet crosses one router per hop, and every router subtracts one from its hop count (TTL); at zero it is dropped, so a long trip needs enough hops of life to begin with.
Every router along the way needs a signpost toward the destination — one missing or wrong signpost strands the packet.
Set the whole chain, and give the packet the life to reach the end.
levels.task: Trace the complete route there and back. Make the forwarding entries and hop limit consistent with that path.

edits.prompt: How many hops of life (TTL) each packet leaves with:
Router 1's signpost for the server's block (10.0.3.0/24):
Router 2's signpost for the server's block (10.0.3.0/24):

goal.text: All three pings cross town and get a reply.

bonus.text: No packet runs out of hops or hits a dead end.

quiz.question: With the signposts all correct, why did the packets still fail until you raised the hop count?
options: Three routers each subtract one, so two hops of life run out before the packet reaches the far side.
A low hop count makes routers forget their signposts.
The server ignores packets with a small hop count.
quiz.why: The hop count is a safety limit, not an address. Each of the three routers decrements it; start with only two and the packet dies in transit, however perfect the routes are.

levels.debrief: The archive confirmed the report. The city route is ready for heavier work.

levels.title: An unknown neighbor
levels.story: The shop knows the printer’s IP address. Its address cache is empty, so the first frame cannot be prepared yet.
concept: A frame is addressed by MAC, not by IP.
ARP finds the MAC for an IP: a broadcast asks everyone on the block.
Only the device that owns that IP answers.
levels.task: Inspect the cache and the devices on this block. Prepare a neighbor query, then trace the response.

edits.prompt: Whose hardware address should the PC ask for?

goal.text: The PC gets the printer's address back.

bonus.text: No more than 4 frames: a broadcast out, one reply back.

quiz.question: The question went to everyone on the block, but only the printer replied. Why?
options: Each device checks the asked-for IP against its own and answers only if it matches.
The switch picked the printer.
The printer was first in line.
quiz.why: A broadcast reaches all, but only the owner of that address recognises it and sends its MAC back.

levels.debrief: The printer was identified. The computer has the local address it needed.

levels.title: Open the service desk
levels.story: The city help desk is online, but its client has not opened a connection. The first attempt is incomplete.
concept: SYN says 'let's talk, my number is x'.
SYN-ACK says 'alright, my number is y, and I heard your x'.
The ACK must acknowledge the server's number: y plus one.
levels.task: Inspect the endpoint ports and sequence cards. Arrange the opening exchange before sending it.

edits.prompt: The PC's first message:
What the PC's third message acknowledges:

goal.text: The connection opens and the page comes back.

bonus.text: The server never has to reset the connection.

quiz.question: Why does the third message acknowledge y + 1 rather than y?
options: An acknowledgement names the next byte expected, which is one past what was received.
y is already taken.
The server counts from one.
quiz.why: TCP acknowledges by naming the next sequence number it wants, so hearing y means asking for y + 1.

levels.debrief: The connection is open. The client can now ask for the service record.

levels.title: A missing page
levels.story: The shop needs a six-part document. The line drops an occasional frame, and the file never arrives in one uninterrupted run.
concept: A window is how many segments may be unacknowledged at once.
A timeout resends from the first one still unacknowledged (go-back-N).
The receiver only accepts segments in order and acknowledges the run it has.
levels.task: Inspect the loss trace. Predict which parts the teaching sender will resend, then choose a transfer plan.

edits.prompt: How many parts in flight at once (the window)?
How long to wait before resending (the timeout)?

goal.text: All six parts arrive, in order.
The transfer finishes within 50 ticks.

bonus.text: No more than 8 parts have to be resent.

quiz.question: With go-back-N, what happens to parts 4 and 5 if part 3 is lost?
options: They are resent too, because the sender goes back to the first unacknowledged part.
Only part 3 is resent; 4 and 5 are kept.
The whole transfer restarts from part 1.
quiz.why: Go-back-N resends everything from the oldest unacknowledged segment onward, since the receiver dropped the ones that arrived out of order.

levels.debrief: The document arrived intact. The delivery record shows the cost of the lost parts.

levels.title: The catalogue download
levels.story: The market catalogue is larger than the last document. Sending one piece at a time is slow, and sending too much makes every loss expensive.
concept: The window is how many parts may be in flight before any are acknowledged — a bigger window keeps the line busier.
On a loss, go-back-N resends everything from the oldest unacknowledged part, so too large a window wastes effort when the link is lossy.
The timeout must be long enough not to resend a part that was only delayed, short enough to recover quickly when one is truly lost.
levels.task: Study the baseline trace. Choose a window and timeout, and state what you expect to change.

edits.prompt: How many parts in flight at once (the window)?
How long to wait before resending (the timeout)?

goal.text: All eight parts arrive, in order.
The download finishes within 70 ticks.

bonus.text: No more than 10 parts have to be resent.

quiz.question: Why can firing all eight parts at once actually be slower here than sending four?
options: When a part is lost, go-back-N resends it and everything after it, so a larger window means a bigger pile to resend on each loss.
The server can only hold one part at a time.
Eight parts always collide with each other.
quiz.why: A window keeps the line busy, but on a lossy link every loss forces a resend of the whole run behind it. The sweet spot keeps the pipe full without making each loss expensive.

levels.debrief: The catalogue reached the shop. The record shows how much work the line repeated.

levels.title: A connection across town
levels.story: The customer’s browser needs the city service desk. A router sits between them, but the conversation still has two endpoints.
concept: A connection opens with three messages: the client's SYN, the server's SYN-ACK, and the client's ACK.
The acknowledgement names the next number expected — one past what was heard.
None of this changes across a router: the handshake is end to end, so it only needs the right destination and the right steps.
levels.task: Trace the packet through the router and build the client-server opening exchange.

edits.prompt: Where is the connection aimed?

options.label: At the web server, over the router (10.0.2.80)

edits.prompt: The PC's first message:
What the PC's third message acknowledges:

goal.text: The connection opens and the page comes back.

bonus.text: The server never has to reset the connection.

quiz.question: The server sat on a different block, reached through a router. How did that change the handshake?
options: Not at all — TCP runs end to end, so the three steps are the same however many routers sit between.
The router had to complete its own handshake first.
The ACK had to name the router's number instead of the server's.
quiz.why: Routers forward packets; they do not take part in the connection. The handshake is strictly between the two ends, so crossing a network changes nothing about it.

levels.debrief: The page returned across town. The router forwarded it without joining the conversation.

levels.title: The final report
levels.story: The market closes in an hour. The last report is eight parts long, and the line beyond the bridge is unreliable.
concept: Reliability and routing work together: the route decides where the parts go, the window and timeout decide how well they survive a lossy link.
A missing signpost strands the transfer no matter how well it is tuned.
Over a lossy link, the window must be large enough to keep moving but small enough that each loss is cheap to recover.
levels.task: Trace the forwarding path, then plan the transfer. Both decisions must work together.

edits.prompt: Router 1's signpost for the server's block (10.0.3.0/24):
How many parts in flight at once (the window)?
How long to wait before resending (the timeout)?

goal.text: All eight parts arrive across town, in order.
The transfer finishes within 110 ticks.

bonus.text: No more than 12 parts have to be resent.

quiz.question: Why does this transfer need both the right route and the right window — neither alone?
options: The route decides whether the parts reach the server at all; the window and timeout decide whether they get there in time over the lossy last link.
The route sets the speed and the window sets the direction.
Either one fixes everything; two settings are just a safety margin.
quiz.why: Routing is about reachability, reliability is about coping with loss. Get the signpost wrong and nothing arrives; get the window wrong and it arrives too slowly. A real transfer needs both.

levels.debrief: The full report reached the market. The town is ready for the night.

levels.title: The night market crowd
levels.story: The night market opens. Five places send legitimate requests to one small server at once. The server link is the busiest part of the city.
concept: Every link carries only so many frames per tick, and every device can hold only so many waiting in line before it must drop the next one.
When requests arrive faster than the server's link can carry them, the queue fills and the extra requests are thrown away — lost, not served.

That is what a denial-of-service attack abuses: not a clever trick, just more requests than the target can answer. The defence is more capacity, or turning the flood away before it reaches the server — rate limits and filtering further out.
levels.task: Inspect the queue, predict where requests will wait, then watch the rush. Record what the bottleneck did.

goal.text: Run the flood and watch it reach the server.

bonus.text: Stay to the end and see how many requests the server never got.

quiz.question: In this setup, why are so many requests dropped?
options: More requests arrive each tick than the single switch-to-server cable can carry, so the queue fills and the rest are dropped.
The requests are addressed to the wrong server.
The server crashed and stopped answering.
The switch is broken and should be a hub instead.
quiz.why: No address is wrong and nothing is broken. The server's one link has a fixed capacity; five senders at once exceed it, the switch's queue for that cable fills, and every frame past the limit is dropped. More senders would only drop more — which is exactly how a flood denies service.

levels.debrief: The rush is over. Some requests were served, and some were lost. The log shows where capacity ran out.
